name: GHK-Cu skin protocol

card.summary: Using the copper peptide GHK-Cu, topically or by injection in peptide circles, to try to improve skin quality, scarring and hair.
card.note: Injectable GHK-Cu is an unapproved research-compound use; topical GHK-Cu is a common cosmetic ingredient.

quick.overview:
GHK-Cu is a copper-binding tripeptide found in human plasma and used in cosmetics under the name copper tripeptide-1. Skin protocols built on it aim for firmer, smoother skin, better wound and post-procedure healing, and in some cases hair.

Lab studies show it stimulates collagen and glycosaminoglycan production in fibroblasts, and small human trials report anti-wrinkle and post-laser effects. Reviews note that data on skin penetration and effectiveness are limited.
quick.how: The commonly discussed route is topical serums and creams, sometimes with microneedling; some peptide communities also discuss injectable forms. Results are described over weeks to months.
quick.risks: Topical products are generally cosmetic; injected or self-compounded forms are outside approved use, with sterility and quality concerns discussed in community threads. Evidence in humans is limited.

lead: The GHK-Cu skin protocol refers to routines built around the peptide GHK-Cu (glycyl-L-histidyl-L-lysine bound to copper) for skin and hair appearance. It is used topically in anti-aging products, and in peptide communities some discuss injection or microneedling with it.[2][3]

Loren Pickart isolated it from human plasma albumin in 1973, and it was identified as a tripeptide in 1977.[1] Cell studies show collagen and glycosaminoglycan stimulation.[4][5] Levels in plasma reportedly decline from about 200 ng/ml at age 20 to about 80 ng/ml by age 60.[6]

A randomised trial of copper-tripeptide skin care after CO2 laser resurfacing was published in 2006.[7] A 2025 review concluded cell data support GHK as an anti-wrinkle ingredient but that skin permeability and effectiveness data are insufficient.[2]

chain: Firmer, smoother skin and faster healing
angle.text: Users apply it to improve fine lines, texture and recovery after resurfacing or microneedling.

paras: In cell studies GHK-Cu stimulated collagen synthesis in fibroblast cultures and increased glycosaminoglycans.[4][5] A review describes stimulation of blood vessel and nerve outgrowth and anti-inflammatory actions.[3]

A randomised controlled trial studied skin care with or without GHK-Cu after CO2 laser resurfacing.[7] Wikipedia reports several small, short controlled facial trials with anti-wrinkle results.[1] A 2025 review states wider evidence on permeability and effectiveness is insufficient.[2] A phase 2 trial of topical GHK-Cu gel for acute wounds is recruiting.[8]
looksmax.org has threads on GHK-Cu for skin, microneedling and acne, and on potency and reconstitution questions.[9][10] These are user discussions, not clinical guidance.

timeline.event: RCT of copper tripeptide after laser resurfacing.[7]
